summary: The note surveys how technology is reshaping geriatric care as the baby boomer generation ages, as of September 2023. It covers remote monitoring, wearables, telemedicine, cognitive apps, robotic companions, smart homes, AI diagnostics, EHRs, VR therapy and mobile clinics, with quotes from clinicians and family members. It concludes that technology can improve quality of life and independence for older adults.
one_line: Overview of technologies such as remote monitoring, wearables, telemedicine, AI, robots, VR and mobile clinics improving health, safety and independence for the elderly.
key_facts: As of September 2023, the note describes technologies enhancing elderly lives amid a growing elderly population as baby boomers age.
Remote health monitoring devices like heart rate and blood pressure monitors relay vital information in real-time to health care providers.
Dr. Jane Smith of the New Cascade Elderly Care Facility says, "With remote monitoring, interventions can be timely, reducing emergency visits."
Pharma companies are developing smart pill dispensers that remind the elderly to take medication, reducing missed doses or overdosing.
87-year-old John Doe's smartwatch alerted his son when he fell in the garden last October, and the son arrived within minutes.
Telemedicine reduces the risk of hospital-acquired infections, and platforms now offer multiuser video calls so family members can join care discussions.
Dr. Robert Huang of the Brain Health Institute says regular mental exercises can slow the progression of disorders like Alzheimer's.
Robots in some assisted living communities reduce loneliness by conversing, playing music and giving reminders, and can guide physical therapy exercises.
Anne Patterson installed a smart home system for her aging mother, who feels in control of her environment.
Dr. Eric Thompson says AI can identify patterns humans may overlook, leading to earlier diagnosis of diseases like Parkinson's or dementia.
Electronic Health Records are described as the backbone of patient care coordination; Dr. Susan O'Malley says they eliminate much guesswork in emergencies.
VR is used for pain management, rehabilitation and easing anxiety and depression symptoms.
The "Wellness on Wheels" mobile clinic toured rural communities last November, providing care and screenings for hundreds of elderly residents.
